query: Earlier studies established BCC refractory high-entropy alloys such as MoNbTaW and MoNbTaVW with excellent high-temperature mechanical properties, while systems including AlNbTiV, NbHfTiV, and AlCrNbTiV also showed favorable mechanical behavior. NbZrTi-based alloys provide broad scope for regulating composition and properties, but changes in elemental identity and proportion can alter both phase constitution and mechanical performance. Equiatomic NbZrTiHfMo is a disordered BCC solid solution with a room-temperature compressive yield strength of 1719 MPa; however, its high Mo content increases the electronegativity difference and is associated with reduced plasticity. Given the constraint of preserving high strength while improving plasticity under room-temperature compression, what single intervention could overcome this limitation? State one hypothesis that identifies the intervention and its mechanism, predicts quantitative or directional changes relative to equiatomic NbZrTiHfMo, defines the conditions and limits of the effect, cites supporting evidence from the prior results summarized above, and proposes an experiment with explicit observations that would falsify the hypothesis.

generation.hypothesis: Partial substitution of Mo by Nb in equiatomic NbZrTiHfMo alloys will improve room‐temperature compressive plasticity while retaining high strength. By reducing the Mo content that causes a high electronegativity difference, the lattice friction impeding dislocation movement is lowered, and replacing it with Nb—which has been shown to enhance ductility—will maintain solid solution strengthening of the BCC phase, mediated by a reduction in the lattice electronegativity mismatch.
generation.material_initial_state: Equiatomic NbZrTiHfMo forming a disordered BCC solid solution with a high Mo content (yield strength ≈1719 MPa) but limited plasticity.
generation.intervention: Reduce the Mo content by partially substituting Mo with additional Nb (adjusting the Nb:Mo ratio) without altering the overall refractory alloy base.
generation.conditions: Room-temperature uniaxial compression tests are conducted on alloys processed under identical conditions to ensure a single-phase disordered BCC structure; the substitution level should be kept moderate to avoid destabilizing the phase.
generation.structural_mediator: A reduction in lattice electronegativity mismatch and lattice distortion due to decreased Mo content and increased Nb content, which moderates the resistance to dislocation motion.
generation.mechanism: High Mo concentration increases the electronegativity difference and lattice friction, reducing plasticity. By partially replacing Mo with Nb, the alloy retains solid solution strengthening while lowering barriers for dislocation mobility, leading to improved ductility under compressive loading.
generation.predicted_outcome: An increase in room-temperature fracture strain (plasticity enhanced, e.g., a relative increase of ≥10%) with only a minor decrease (within about 10%) in compressive yield strength compared to the 1719 MPa baseline.
generation.baseline: Equiatomic NbZrTiHfMo with a compressive yield strength of approximately 1719 MPa and limited room-temperature plasticity.
generation.boundary: Excessive reduction of Mo or over-enrichment of Nb might lead to phase instability or loss of high strength; the beneficial effect is expected only within a moderate substitution range that preserves the disordered BCC structure.
generation.uncertainty: The precise balance between strength retention and ductility improvement requires experimental verification, and the optimal Nb:Mo ratio must be established.

falsification_experiment.design: Prepare a series of NbZrTiHfMo-based alloys with incrementally reduced Mo content (e.g., 0%, 10%, 20%, and 30% reduction in Mo replaced by Nb) under identical melting and homogenization conditions. Conduct room-temperature uniaxial compression tests while monitoring phase purity via XRD and microstructural uniformity via SEM.
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If any modified alloy fails to show a statistically significant increase in plasticity (≥10% improvement in fracture strain) while maintaining the yield strength within 10% of the baseline value, or if phase changes or brittle precipitates form due to the substitution, then the hypothesis is falsified.

cited_evidence.text: Refractory high-entropy alloys (RHEAs) are a relatively new class of multicomponent materials that are based on several refractory metals, but may also contain other, generally low density, elements and typically have a body centered cubic (BCC) crystal structure. These alloys have recently received much attention because of their attractive combination of properties not achievable by other classes of metallic alloys. For example, the first two RHEAs, NbMoTaW and NbMoTaVW, showed weak temperature dependence of yield strength in the temperature range from 600 °C to 1600 °C, with yield strength above 400 MPa at 1600 °C,. Unfortunately, these two alloys had high density (>12 g/cm3) and further developments aimed at reducing the alloy density while keeping superior high-temperature properties. In the second generation RHEAs, high-density Ta and W were replaced with lower density refractory elements, such as Cr, Mo, Nb, V and Zr, and low density Al and Ti were added. This resulted in RHEAs with lower densities and high-temperature strengths better than the properties of Ni-based superalloys and Fe-based steels. AbstractNowadays refractory high-entropy alloys (RHEAs) are regarded as great candidates for the replacement of superalloys at high temperature. To design a RHEA, one must understand the pros and cons of every refractory element. However, the elemental effect on mechanical properties remains unclear. In this study, the subtraction method was applied on equiatomic HfMoNbTaTiZr alloys to discover the role of each element, and, thus, HfMoNbTaTiZr, HfNbTaTiZr, HfMoTaTiZr, HfMoNbTiZr, HfMoNbTaZr, and HfMoNbTaTi were fabricated and analyzed. The microstructure and mechanical properties of each alloy at the as-cast state were examined. The solid solution phase formation rule and the solution strengthening effect are also discussed. Finally, the mechanism of how Mo, Nb, Ta, Ti, and Zr affect the HfMoNbTaTiZr alloys was established after comparing the properties of these alloys.Keywords: high-entropy alloys, refractory high-entropy alloys, alloys design, elevated-temperature yield strength, solid solution strengthening effect

The fracture strain increases from 4% for the HfMoTaTiZr alloy to 12% for HfMoNbTaTiZr. The presence of Ta can increase the yield strength but decrease the toughness. Ti seems to have no significant influence on strength, but it has a negative effect on toughness. Zr increases the strength; however, it strongly deteriorates the toughness at room temperature, because the fracture strain decreases from 27% for the HfMoNbTaTi alloy to 12% for HfMoNbTaTiZr. The presence of Mo, which has the highest shear modulus, increases the yield strength at room temperature from 929 MPa to 1512 MPa significantly. Nevertheless, the toughness decreases tremendously, fracture strain declines from > 50% to 12%.
